answers.brief_reasoning: Random assignment to token vs no-token conditions with the independent variable manipulated.
answers.final_answer: Experiment (randomized experiment with random assignment to Token and No-token groups).
The percentage of assigned homework handed in complete during the six weeks.
On average, the Token group completed 18 percentage points more of its assigned homework (82%) than the No-token group (64%), so the Token group completed more homework.

Informed consent/assent: parents gave written permission and each student agreed to take part. (Others: right to withdraw, since students were told they could stop at any time without penalty; confidentiality, since records were identified only by code numbers; IRB approval.)

answers.brief_reasoning: The sample was small and came from only one school.
answers.final_answer: Generalizability is limited. All 100 participants were fifth graders from four classrooms in one public elementary school, and only volunteers whose parents returned permission forms took part. So the results may not apply to other grades, other schools, or other regions. Random assignment supports a causal conclusion within this sample, but it does not make the sample representative of a wider population.

answers.brief_reasoning: The difference is in the predicted direction and is statistically significant.
answers.final_answer: The findings support the hypothesis. The Token group's mean completion (82%) was higher than the No-token group's (64%), and the researchers reported that this difference was statistically significant, so it is unlikely to be due to chance. Because students were randomly assigned, the higher completion can be attributed to earning tokens.

answers.brief_reasoning: Variables measured, not manipulated; correlation computed.
answers.final_answer: Correlational study (survey-based correlational research).
Perceived stress = the student's total score (10–50) on a 10-item questionnaire about how overwhelmed the student felt during the past month.
r = -0.46 shows a moderate negative correlation: students with higher social support scores tended to have lower perceived stress scores. It does not show that one causes the other.

answers.brief_reasoning: Several guidelines are described in the study.
answers.final_answer: Informed consent: students read a consent statement before starting the survey. (Other acceptable answers: the right to withdraw, since students could close the survey at any time; confidentiality/anonymity, since answers were stored under code numbers and names were not collected; or IRB approval.)

The findings are of limited generalizability. All participants were first-year students at one university, and they were self-selected: only 150 of the 900 students who were emailed (about 17%) completed the survey. So the sample may not represent all first-year students, or even all first-years at that university. Students who chose to respond may differ in stress or support from those who did not. The sample of 150 gives some basis for generalizing to similar students at that school.

The findings support the hypothesis. The correlation of r = -0.46 is negative, meaning students who reported more social support tended to report less perceived stress, which is the direction the hypothesis predicted. Because the study is correlational, it shows an association, not that social support reduces stress.

answers.brief_reasoning: A defensible claim the sources support.
answers.final_answer: Yes. The district should move the high school start time later, because a later start lets adolescents get more sleep, and more sleep improves the attention they need for learning.
Source 1: students randomly assigned to 8 hours in bed scored 85% mean accuracy on the attention task, versus 71% for students given 6 hours. The difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Sleep deprivation and selective attention; random assignment allows a causal conclusion.
answers.final_answer: Students were randomly assigned to conditions, so sleep amount was the manipulated independent variable. That lets us conclude that sleep deprivation caused worse selective attention, meaning less ability to pick out targets among distractors. Paying attention is the first step in encoding information into memory. Teens who are short on sleep in class will therefore encode and learn less, which supports a later start that protects their sleep.
Source 2: students in the district starting at 8:45 a.m. reported an average of 7.6 hours of sleep on school nights. Students in the district starting at 7:15 a.m. reported 6.4 hours.

answers.brief_reasoning: Circadian rhythm phase delay in adolescence.
answers.final_answer: During puberty, teens' circadian rhythm shifts later (a sleep phase delay), so melatonin is released later and they cannot easily fall asleep early. With an early start, they cut sleep short and build up a sleep debt. The later-start district's students got about 1.2 more hours of sleep, which fits a schedule that matches their biological clock. This is correlational data and the districts may differ in other ways, such as income. Still, it agrees with the circadian explanation and with the experiment in Source 1.

answers.final_answer: Social media platforms should hide like counts, because hiding them reduces teenagers' worry about how others judge them and the pressure to compare themselves with others.
Source 1: Teenagers randomly assigned to the Hidden version had a mean worry rating of 5.2, compared with 6.8 in the Visible version. The difference was statistically significant.

answers.brief_reasoning: Experiment allows a causal conclusion; social comparison theory explains it.
answers.final_answer: Because teenagers were randomly assigned to the two versions, the groups were probably similar at the start. That means hiding counts (the independent variable) likely caused the lower worry (the dependent variable). Social comparison theory explains why: visible like counts give teens a number to use for upward comparison with peers, which makes them more anxious about how they are seen. Taking the number away removes that cue, so worry goes down, which supports hiding likes.
Source 3: 19 of the 30 teenagers interviewed said they felt less pressure to post only popular photos after like counts were hidden for one month.

Operant conditioning explains this result. Likes work as a positive reinforcer that comes on a variable-ratio schedule, so teens learn to post whatever earns the most likes. When counts are hidden, that reinforcement is no longer shown, so the learned behavior weakens (extinction). Teens then feel less pressure to post only popular photos, which supports hiding likes. (One limit: the interviewees volunteered and may have had stronger opinions, and 11 of 30 still compared themselves in other ways, so the effect is real but not complete.)
